### **23.3.1 Population genetics**

1.  Calculate a PRS for each participant. Which participant has the highest PRS? The lowest?

```{r}
longer_ca_co_genotypes <- ca_co_genotypes |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("locus_"),
    names_to = "risk_locus",
    values_to = "risk_genotype_dosage"
  ) |> 
  left_join(
    gwas_top_hits |> 
      dplyr::select(locus, beta), #select the locus and beta row
    by = join_by(risk_locus == locus)
    )
#make it easier to do following calculation
One_locus_score <- longer_ca_co_genotypes |> 
  mutate(
    one_locus_score = risk_genotype_dosage*beta
  ) 
#calculate the locus score for each individual locus
PRS<-One_locus_score |> 
  summarise(
    Polygenic_risk_score = sum(one_locus_score),
    .by = c(donorid, status)
    )
#calculate the PRS for each participant
PRS |> 
  slice_max(Polygenic_risk_score, n = 1) #participant with the highest PRS
PRS |> 
  slice_min(Polygenic_risk_score, n = 1) #participant with the lowest PRS
#the participant with the highest PRS is 2.389 and the donorID is d249 (control)
#the participant with the lowest PRS is 0.172 and the donorID is d205 (case)
```

2.  Plot and describe (with descriptive statistics) the distribution of PRS for both cases and controls.

```{r}
PRS |> 
  summarise(
    min_PRS = min(Polygenic_risk_score),
    max_PRS = max(Polygenic_risk_score),
    mean_PRS = mean(Polygenic_risk_score),
    median_PRS = median(Polygenic_risk_score),
    sd_PRS = sd(Polygenic_risk_score),
    .by = status
  ) # descriptive statistics of the distribution of PRS for both cases and controls
ggplot(
  data = PRS,
  aes(x = Polygenic_risk_score, fill = status))+
  geom_histogram(bins = 15,
                 colour = "white",
                 linewidth = 0.3) + # creating a histogram that range into 15 bars, choose 15 is because it is much smoother compare to bins=30 which is the default, and easier to see overall distribution
  facet_wrap(~status) + # make two separate plots based on the status
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("case" = "#D96B5F", "ctrl" = "#4C84A6")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Polygenic Risk Scores",
    subtitle = "Parkinson's disease cases and healthy controls",
    x = "Polygenic risk score (PRS)",
    y = "Number of participants",
    ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none", # remove the legend because the groups are already labelled
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), # make the main title more prominent
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, colour = "grey40"), # smaller, muted subtitle to make visual hierarchy
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"), # add a light grey background to facet labels
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11), # make facet labels easy to distinguish
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"), # emphasise axis titles
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "black") # use black axis text for clear contrast
  )

ggplot(PRS, aes(x = status, y = Polygenic_risk_score, fill = status)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.5,
    alpha = 0.85,
    outlier.shape = 21,
    outlier.size = 2
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
  values = c("case" = "#D96B5F", "ctrl" = "#4C84A6") # set consistent colours for cases and controls
) +
labs(
  title = "Polygenic Risk Scores by Disease Status",
  x = "Disease status",
  y = "Polygenic risk score (PRS)"
) + # add the plot title and axis labels
theme_classic(base_size = 12) + # use a simple theme with consistent font size
theme(
  legend.position = "none", # remove the legend
  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), # make the title bold
  axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"), # make axis titles bold
  axis.text = element_text(colour = "black") # set axis text to black
)

#case group have higher mean and median PRS, with slightly greater standard deviation (variation) compare to the control group. The distributions of both group overlap substantially, hence the PRS cannot be perfectly distinguish case from control.
#both disttibution are unimodal and symmetric, and both have two outliers, case outliers have the lowest PRS and the control outliers have the higher PRS
```

3.  Is there a statistically significant difference in the PRS of cases and controls? Ensure you check all the assumptions of the test you choose.

```{r}
# check normality visually
ggplot(PRS, aes(sample=Polygenic_risk_score)) +
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line() +
  facet_wrap(~status) +
  labs(
    title = "Normal Q-Q Plot of PRS",
    x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
    y = "Sample Quantiles"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
# QQ-plot does suggest normality for both case and control, a shapiro-wilk test will confirm this finding

PRS |> 
  filter(status == "case") |> 
  pull(Polygenic_risk_score) |> 
  shapiro.test()

PRS |> 
  filter(status == "ctrl") |> 
  pull(Polygenic_risk_score) |> 
  shapiro.test()
# for case, the p value is 0.2129, no evidence against normality
# for ctrl, the p value is 0.007452, strong evidence against normality
# to do a t-test, both group need to meet the normality assumption, since the ctrl group has violated the assumption, Wilcoxon rank-sum test will be applied here to compare the two groups instead of t-test.

wilcox.test(Polygenic_risk_score ~ status, data = PRS)
# the wilcoxon test statistics value is 15554 with a p-value of 1.013e-08. This suggests a extremely strong evidence that the PRS distribution differ between the Parkinson disease case group and the control group, with case group have higher PRS compare to the control group.
```

### **23.3.2 RNA-seq of patient iPSC-derived neurons**

Firstly, load the packages

```{r}
library(edgeR)
library(RNAseq123)
library(limma)
library(pheatmap)
library(ggrepel)
```

1.  Which genes are differentially expressed between PD cases and healthy controls? Please also visualise your DE results with appropriate plot(s).

```{r}
# Firstly, we need to filter our lowly expressed genes to increase our statistical power. To do this, we will use the filterByExpr() function in the edgeR package. This will keep genes with a count of 10 or more in at least 8 samples (as we have 8 samples per group)
  keep <- filterByExpr(dge)
# To check the proportion of genes we have ommited, we can create a proportions table:
  proportions(table(keep)) #We are keeping 97.77% of our genes
# to apply this filter to the DGE object, we will use [] to filter out FALSE hits (lowly expressed genes) and assign this dge
  dge <- dge[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]

# Now we need to normalise our data by converting it to counts per million (CPM), so we can compare samples and groups, and account for RNA composition bias. To do this we will use the TMM method to calculate the normalisation factor for each sample. normLibSizes() function can be used to calculate normalisation factors
  dge <- normLibSizes(dge, method = "TMM")
# the normalisation factors in dge$samples are close to 1 in all samples, suggesting minimal difference in RNA composition between samples

# Now we will fit a linear model using the limma-voom framework 

  # By first creating a design matrix to represent covariates
  design <- model.matrix(~0 + group, data = dge$samples)

  # We will then need to rename our design matrix to be cleaner
  colnames(design) <- c("Control", "Case")

  # Now make contrast matrix
  contr_matrix <- makeContrasts(
    CasevsControl = "Case - Control",
    levels = design
  )
  # creates mean-variance relationship plot to check voom
  v <- voom(dge, design, plot = TRUE)
  
  # applies linear model to mean variance
  vfit <- lmFit(v)
  
  # apply constrasts, calculating coefficients for CasevsControl contrast
  vfit <- contrasts.fit(vfit, contrasts = contr_matrix)
  
  # statistical test: emnpirical bayes moderated T-test
  efit <- eBayes(vfit)
  
  #decide tests function to decide if a gene is differentially expressed or not with multiple testing correction
  dt <- decideTests(efit)

  summary(dt)
  
  top <- topTable(efit, coef = "CasevsControl", number = Inf)
  #converted to tibble to make it easier to work with
  top_tibble <- as_tibble(top)

# ggplot MA plot
  # first need to assign gene names to the efit$genes dataframe
  
  # turning efit$genes into character
  efit$genes$genes <- as.character(efit$genes$genes)
  # so I can now change efit$genes to include SYMBOL column which matches the entrez_genename_key#entrezid to efit$genes$genes, and supplies the entrez_genename_key$gene_name to the efit$genes dataframe
  efit$genes$SYMBOL <- entrez_genename_key$gene_name[
    match(efit$genes$genes, entrez_genename_key$entrezid)]

  # now organise data from efit into a tibble format
  ma_plot_data <- tibble(logFC = efit$coefficients[, "CasevsControl"],
                       AvgExpr = efit$Amean,
                       status = factor(as.numeric(dt[, "CasevsControl"])),
                       gene = efit$genes$SYMBOL,
                      p_value = efit$p.value[, "CasevsControl"])

ma_plot_data_fct <- ma_plot_data %>%
  mutate(
    # replace status with a new factor
    status = factor(
      status,
      # levels (order is not DE, down, up)
      levels = c(0, -1, 1),
      # labels for the numbers so they are readble
      labels = c("Not DE", "Down", "Up")
    )
  )
# labelling of top most significant genes
top_de_genes <- ma_plot_data_fct %>%
  filter(!is.na(gene)) %>%
  slice_min(p_value, n = 39)

# MA ggplot
ggplot(ma_plot_data_fct, aes(x = AvgExpr, y = logFC, colour = status)) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  geom_label_repel(
    data = top_de_genes,
    aes(label = gene),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Not DE" = "grey70",
    "Down" = "#4C84A6",
    "Up" = "#D96B5F"
  )) + # Use consistent colours across plots
  labs(
    title = "MA Plot: PD Cases vs Healthy Controls",
    x = "Average expression",
    y = "Log2 fold change",
    colour = "Expression status"
  ) +
  theme_classic() # Keep the plot style consistent

# Volcano Plot
ggplot(ma_plot_data_fct, aes(x = logFC, y = -log10(p_value), colour = status)) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  geom_label_repel(
    data = top_de_genes,
    aes(label = gene),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Not DE" = "grey70",
    "Down" = "#4C84A6",
    "Up" = "#D96B5F"
  )) + # Use the same colours as the MA plot
  labs(
    title = "Volcano Plot: PD Cases vs Healthy Controls",
    x = "Log2 fold change",
    y = "-Log10(p-value)",
    colour = "Expression status"
  ) +
  theme_classic()

```

2.  Which gene ontology families do the DE genes belong to?

```{r}
#use top_de_genes, join gene_ontology
#first join top_de_genes with entrez_id
top_de_genes <- top_de_genes |> na.omit() |> 
  mutate(gene_name = gene)

top_de_genes_id <- left_join(
  top_de_genes, entrez_genename_key) |> 
  mutate(entrezgene_id = entrezid) |> 
  dplyr::select(-entrezid) # Remove the original ID column
 
#now join top_de_genes_id with gene_ontology
top_de_gene_ontology <- top_de_genes_id |> left_join(gene_ontology) 

top_de_gene_ontology |> slice_min(p_value, n = 39) |> dplyr::select(gene, status, desc)
```

3.  Is the clustering of samples by gene expression consistent with their disease status as cases and controls?

From this multi-dimensional scale (MDS) plot, we can see that 5/8 cases cluster together on the left, and all the controls cluster to the right. Interestingly, 3/8 cases cluster to the left where the controls are. This raises concerns about a potential batch effect or mislabeling of samples, as the clustering of samples by gene expression is not always consistent with disease status.

```{r}
#Now we want to check that our samples group together as we'd expect based on our experimental design, by making an MDS plot. This will show us whether or not the controls group together, and the PD patients group together. To do this, we will use the plotMDS() function and then make the MDS plot in ggplot2
mds_result <- plotMDS(dge)
#create tibble
mds_tibble <- tibble(
  x = mds_result$x,
  y = mds_result$y,
  sample = colnames(dge),
  group = dge$samples$group
)
#
dim1_var_explained <- round(mds_result$var.explained[1] * 100)
dim2_var_explained <- round(mds_result$var.explained[2] * 100)

# Create MDS plot
ggplot(mds_tibble, aes(x = x, y = y, colour = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) + # show sample clustering
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = sample), size = 3, box.padding = 0.5,
  point.padding = 0.2) + # label samples, reduce overlap between labels
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "case" = "#D96B5F",
    "control" = "#4C84A6"
  )) + # Keep colours consistent across plots
  labs(
    title = "MDS Plot of Gene Expression",
    x = paste0("Leading logFC dimension 1 (", dim1_var_explained, "%)"),
    y = paste0("Leading logFC dimension 2 (", dim2_var_explained, "%)"),
    colour = "Disease status"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "black")
  )
```

### **23.3.3 Drug screening**

1.  Using the `geom_tile()` function, visualise the luminescence across the plate. Do there appear to be any spatial patterns in this data?

```{r}
# Convert the plate data to long format, with each row representing one well.
plate1_long <- plate1 |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = contains("col"),
    names_to = "column",
    values_to = "RLU"
  ) |> 
  # create numeric row and column coordinates for plotting
  mutate(
    row_num = as.numeric(str_remove(plate_row, "row")),
    col_num = as.numeric(str_remove(column, "col"))
  )

# Heat map
ggplot(plate1_long, aes(x = col_num, y = row_num, fill = RLU)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "lightblue", high = "darkblue", limits = c(429, 742), breaks = seq(400, 750, by = 50)) +
  labs(
    title = "Luminescence across the 1536-well plate",
    x = "Column",
    y = "Row",
    fill = "Luminescence (RLU)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Most values have relatively similar luminescence values.
# A few individual wells have much higher luminescence, coloured with dark blue.
# No obvious consistent gradient from one side of the plate to the other. 
# No obvious edge effect where wells around the edges are consistently higher or lower.
```

2.  Which compounds are statistically significantly associated with increased neuronal viability after MPP exposure? Ensure that you check your assumptions.

```{r}
# Convert the plate_meta data to long format, with each row representing one well.
plate_meta_long <- plate_meta |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = contains("col"),
    names_to = "column",
    values_to = "compound"
  )

# Combine the luminescence results with compound information based on each well's row and column.
drug_data <- plate_meta_long |> 
  left_join(
    plate1_long,
    by = c("plate_row", "column")
  )

# Separate the compound ID from the test/control label at the last underscore.
drug_data <- drug_data |> 
  mutate(
    group = str_extract(compound, "test|ctrl"),
    compound = str_remove(compound, "_(test|ctrl)$")
  )

# Summarise luminescence by test and control groups.
compound_summary <- drug_data |> 
  summarise (
    mean_RLU = mean(RLU),
    median_RLU = median(RLU),
    sd_RLU = sd(RLU),
    n = n(),
    .by = c(compound, group)
  ) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = group,
    values_from = c(mean_RLU, median_RLU, sd_RLU)
  ) |> # Put test and control results side by side for each compound.
  mutate(
    difference = mean_RLU_test - mean_RLU_ctrl
  ) # Calculate the difference in mean RLU between test and control groups.

# Welch's t-test assumption checking
# First, check the normality of RLU for some compounds
drug_data |> 
  filter(compound %in% c( "cmpd_6406", "cmpd_4834", "cmpd_6255")) |> 
  ggplot(aes(sample = RLU)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  facet_wrap(~compound + group)
# The QQ plots show no obvious deviation from normality across these compounds. However, normality is difficult to confirm with only four replicates per group.

#Perform Welch's t-test without assuming equal variances.
t_test_results <- drug_data |> 
  summarise(
    p_value = t.test(RLU ~group, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value,
    .by = compound
  )
# Adjust p-values for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method.
t_test_results <- t_test_results |> 
  mutate(
    p_adjusted = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH")
  )

# Combine t-test results with compound summary information
t_test_results <- t_test_results |> 
  left_join(
    compound_summary |> 
      dplyr::select(compound, difference), # Keep only the compound ID and mean RLU difference.
    by = "compound"
  )
# Find significant compounds associated with increased neuronal viability.
t_test_results |> 
  filter(p_adjusted < 0.05,
         difference > 0)

# Conclusion: Four compounds (cmpd_5386, cmpd_5118, cmpd_7466 and cmpd_6972) significantly increased neuronal viability after MPP exposure.
```

3.  What are the mechanisms of action and targets of the compounds you identify in Q2?

```{r}
# Find the target and mechanism of action for the significant compounds.
compound_dict |> 
  filter(id %in% c("cmpd_5386", "cmpd_5118", "cmpd_7466", "cmpd_6972"))

# Combine significant compounds with their targets and mechanisms of action.
question3_results <- t_test_results |> 
  filter(p_adjusted < 0.05, difference > 0) |> 
  left_join(
    compound_dict,
    by = c("compound" = "id")
  )
```

### **23.3.4 Clinical trial**

1.  Plot each participants’ gait data and describe it using descriptive statistics. Which of these descriptive statistics do you think is most useful for capturing the overall gait smoothness and balance of a participant?

The participants' mean gait measurements across the 700 seconds ranges from approximately -0.91° to 0.78°, showing that on average, their orientations are close to upright (0°). The median measurements, ranging from approximately -1.40° to 0.49°, also indicate this. However, because the individual measurements range from approximately -50° to 61°, it shows that some measurements deviate considerably from upright (0°) in both directions. Additionally, the standard deviations range from approximately 2° to 17°, indicating that the gait measurements vary considerably across the 700 seconds.

Absolute mean gait measurements range from approximately 2° to 14°, indicating that the average magnitude of deviation from upright is greater than the mean values suggest. This is because absolute mean accounts for the magnitude of deviations regardless of direction and prevents positive and negative values to cancel each other, as can happen with mean calculations. Therefore, this statistic is most useful for capturing the overall gait smoothness and balance. It also best reflects the differences observed in the plots. For example, participant d056 has the highest absolute mean (approximately 14°) and appears to show the greatest deviation from 0° in their plot. However, absolute mean only measures the average magnitude of deviation from upright and does not directly show how smoothly participants' gait changes across the 700 seconds.

```{r}

load("~/Desktop/group3_data/gait.Rda")
View(gait_data)

#check for missing data
any(is.na(gait_data))


# carry out data wrangling to make plotting and calculations easier 

# Reshape into longer data by moving the 700 seconds columns into a single column 

gait_long <- gait_data |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = contains("_sec"), 
    names_to = "time", 
    values_to = "gait"
  )   
 
  
  # separate values in "time" column from units and make them into numeric character
  
gait_long <- gait_long |>  separate(
    time, 
    into = c("time", "units"), 
    sep = "_"
  ) 
  
gait_long <- gait_long |>  mutate(time = as.numeric(time)) 
  class(gait_long$time)


# plot each participant's gait measurements across the 700 seconds
# horizontal line at 0 represents perfectly upright orientation

ggplot( gait_long, aes(x = time, y= gait)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "blue") + 
  facet_wrap(~ donorid) +
  labs(
    x = "Time (seconds)",
    y = "Vertical orientation (degrees off-axis)",
    title = "Gait orientation over time for each participant"
  )


#calculate descriptive statistics for all participants

gait_summary <- gait_long |> 
  group_by(donorid, treatment) |> 
  summarise(
    mean_gait = mean(gait),
    median_gait = median(gait), 
    stand.dev_gait = sd(gait),
    min_gait = min(gait),
    max_gait = max(gait),
    absolute_mean = mean(abs(gait))
    
  ) |>  
  ungroup()
  
View(gait_summary)


```

2.  Is there a statistically significant difference in gait between participants receiving L-DOPA and the new compound? Ensure that you check your assumptions.

The p value (0.03503) is smaller than 0.05, suggesting that there is a statistically significant difference in the absolute mean gait between participants receiving L-DOPA and the new compound. The new compound group has a lower absolute mean gait (5.699946°) than the L-DOPA group (8.762259°), suggesting a smaller average deviation from upright in this group. This indicates that participants receiving the new compound have gait measurements that are, on average, closer to upright, regardless of direction.

```{r}

# Check assumptions for t-test:


# 1. visualise data and check for equal variances between the 2 treatment groups

ggplot(gait_summary, aes(x = treatment, y = absolute_mean)) +
  geom_boxplot() 


# 2. check for normality in both groups

ggplot(gait_summary, aes(sample = absolute_mean)) +
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line() +
  facet_wrap(~treatment)
  
# confirm with a Shapiro-Wilk test in both groups

gait_summary %>%
  filter(treatment == "L-DOPA control") %>%
  pull(absolute_mean) %>% 
  shapiro.test()

gait_summary %>%
  filter(treatment == "New compound") %>%
  pull(absolute_mean) %>% 
  shapiro.test()

# p-values are 0.1284 for L-DOPA group and 0.5617 for New compound group 
# both are greater than 0.05, so insufficient evidence to reject normality



# conduct Welch’s t-test 

t.test(absolute_mean ~ treatment, data = gait_summary, var.equal = FALSE)
```

3.  Does either of age or the exercise regime affect gait? If so, take this into consideration when investigating the relationship between the treatment and gait.

Linear regression modelling shows that there is a significant positive association between age and absolute mean gait (coefficient= 0.272, p = 0.00322) , suggesting that older participants tend to have greater deviations from upright. Exercise is also significantly associated with absolute mean gait (coefficient= -3.0961, p= 0.0321), with participants in the exercise group showing lower average deviations from upright than those who did not exercise.

After adjusting for age and exercise when investigating the relationship between the treatment and gait, the new compound group has an absolute mean gait 2.6922° lower than the L-DOPA group (coefficient= 2.6922, p = 0.000123). This suggests that absolute mean gait remains statistically different between both treatment groups even after accounting for age and exercise.

```{r}


# join gait_summary and  gait_data to include age and excercise information too
  
 joined_data <-  left_join( gait_summary , gait_data , 
             by = join_by(donorid)
    
  )

View(joined_data)

# 1. check relationship between gait and treatment

lm(absolute_mean ~ treatment.x, data = joined_data) %>% summary()

# 2. check relationship between gait and age 

lm(absolute_mean ~ age, data = joined_data) %>% summary()


# 3. check relationship between gait and exercise 

lm(absolute_mean ~ exercise, data = joined_data) %>% summary()

# 4. check relationship between gait and treatment after accounting for age

lm(absolute_mean ~ treatment.x + age, data = joined_data) %>% summary()

# 5. check relationship between gait and treatment after accounting for age and exercise

lm(absolute_mean ~ treatment.x + age + exercise, data = joined_data) %>% summary()
```

#WHAT OTHER FACTOR COULD BE AT PLAY? PGS, AGE, EXERCISE?


ggplot(mds_tibble, aes(x = x, y = y, colour = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) + # show sample clustering
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = sample), size = 3, box.padding = 0.5,
                  point.padding = 0.2) + # label samples, reduce overlap between labels

    "case" = "#D96B5F",

    title = "MDS Plot of Gene Expression",
    x = paste0("Leading logFC dimension 1 (", dim1_var_explained, "%)"),

  )

4.  Is there any relationship between the PRS and gait of patients in the clinical trial?

```{r}
find("select")
select <- dplyr::select#maybe due to laptop issue, find("select") [1] "package:OrganismDbi"   "package:AnnotationDbi" "package:dplyr"   

gait_PRS<-gait_summary |> 
  select(donorid, absolute_mean) |> 
  left_join(
    gait_data |> 
      select(donorid, treatment, age, exercise),
    by=join_by(donorid)
  ) |> 
  left_join(
    PRS |> 
      select(donorid, status, Polygenic_risk_score),
    by=join_by(donorid)
  )

ggplot(
  gait_PRS, aes(x=Polygenic_risk_score, y=absolute_mean, colour=treatment)
)+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method="lm")+
  labs(
    title = "Relationship between PRS and gait in the clinical trial",
    x = "Polygenic risk score",
    y = "Absolute mean deviation from upright",
    colour = "Treatment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
#linear regression
#L-DOPA control: Higher PRS is associated with greater Absolute mean deviation from upright
#New compound: Higher PRS is associated with smaller Absolute mean deviation from upright
#However, the significance is not yet determined

#multiple linear regression model examines whether PRS is associated with Absolute mean deviation from upright, while adjusting for treatment group, age and exercise.
lm_model_PRS_gait<-lm(absolute_mean~Polygenic_risk_score+treatment+age+exercise, data=gait_PRS)
summary(lm_model_PRS_gait)#After adjusting for treatment, age and exercise, PRS was not significantly associated with mean absolute deviation from upright (β = 0.394 per one-unit increase in PRS, SE = 0.364, p = 0.303). This indicates insufficient evidence of an association, rather than proving that no relationship exists.

#assumption for linear model lm_model_PRS_gait
library(lmtest)
plot(lm_model_PRS_gait)#visualise
#it will be hard to tell if the assumption are met visually, the tests are applied
resettest(lm_model_PRS_gait)#Linearity: the reset test found no evidence that the model is not linear with p-value equals to 0.7465
bptest(lm_model_PRS_gait)#Homoscedasticity: The Breusch–Pagan test found no evidence of unequal residual variance (p-value=0.6255)
shapiro.test(lm_model_PRS_gait$residuals)#Normality of residuals: The Shapiro–Wilk test found no evidence that the residuals are not following a normal distribution (p-value=0.4728)
#Independence: Each patient contributed one PRS and one gait summary hence there is only one observation per patient, therefore the independence of errors between patients is met which means one patient’s unexplained gait variation should not be related to another patient’s.
#All four assumptions are met, and hence the liner model for PRS_gait is valid

#multiple linear regression model examines whether PRS is associated with Absolute mean deviation from upright between treatment groups, while adjusting for age and exercise.
lm_model_PRSxtreatment_gait<-lm(absolute_mean~Polygenic_risk_score*treatment+age+exercise, data=gait_PRS)
summary(lm_model_PRSxtreatment_gait)
#After adjusting for age and exercise, there was insufficient evidence that the PRS–gait relationship differed between treatments (p-value = 0.123689)

#assumption for linear model lm_model_PRSxtreatment_gait
plot(lm_model_PRSxtreatment_gait)
resettest(lm_model_PRSxtreatment_gait)#Linearity: the reset test found no evidence that the model is not linear with p-value equals to 0.3589
bptest(lm_model_PRSxtreatment_gait)#Homoscedasticity: The Breusch–Pagan test found no evidence of unequal residual variance (p-value=0.4197)
shapiro.test(lm_model_PRSxtreatment_gait$residuals)#Normality of residuals: The Shapiro–Wilk test found no evidence that the residuals are not following a normal distribution (p-value=0.8745)
#Independence is met as described above
#All four assumptions are met, and hence the liner model for PRSxtreatment_gait is valid.
```
